problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).$

activity_context.topic_title: Further Differentiation of Curves Given in Polar Form

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Polar Curve
examples.problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}$ for the polar curve $r=5.$
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta}.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta.$ 

Using the fact that $r=5,$ we get

$$
x =5\cos\theta, \qquad y=5\sin\theta.
$$

Then, to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
x'(\theta) = -5\sin\theta, \qquad y'(\theta) = 5\cos\theta.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{ 5\cos\theta }{  -5\sin\theta} =-\cot\theta .
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}{-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}{csc}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =(6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =6{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′}-{({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =6(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′} \\  & =6{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′}-\frac{1}{2}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′} \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$
